title: What Is a Stablecoin? A Plain-English Guide
description: What stablecoins are, how they keep a steady value, what they are used for and the risks to know before using USDT, USDC or euro stablecoins.
excerpt: Stablecoins aim to hold a steady value while living on a blockchain. Here is how they work, what they are used for and what to watch out for.
author: Coincashy Editorial Team
html:
Key takeaways

  • A stablecoin is a crypto-asset designed to keep a steady value, usually 1:1 with a currency such as the US dollar or the euro.
  • Most large stablecoins are backed by reserves such as cash and short-term government debt held by the issuer.
  • Stablecoins are useful for payments and settlement, but they still carry risks, including issuer, reserve and regulatory risk.

If you have ever moved money between crypto and a bank account, you have probably come across stablecoins. They sit between the two worlds: they live on blockchains like other crypto-assets, but they aim to hold a steady value like ordinary money. This guide explains what they are, how they keep their value, what they are used for and what to watch out for.

What is a stablecoin?

A stablecoin is a type of crypto-asset whose value is linked, or "pegged", to something stable, most often a national currency. One dollar-linked stablecoin is designed to be worth one US dollar; one euro-linked stablecoin is designed to be worth one euro. The best-known examples are USDT, issued by Tether, and USDC, issued by Circle.

Unlike bitcoin or ether, whose prices move with supply and demand, a stablecoin is built to stay close to its peg. That makes it practical for paying, saving value briefly between transactions, or settling payments across borders.

How do stablecoins keep their value?

There are three common designs:

  • Fiat-backed: the issuer holds reserves, such as bank deposits and short-term government bonds, and allows eligible customers to redeem tokens for money. Most stablecoin volume today uses this model.
  • Crypto-backed: tokens are backed by other crypto-assets locked in smart contracts, usually with more collateral than the tokens issued to absorb price swings.
  • Algorithmic: supply is adjusted by code rather than backed by reserves. Some of these designs have failed in the past, so they are generally considered higher risk.

What are stablecoins used for?

  • Moving between crypto and fiat: many people convert crypto into a stablecoin first, then into money in their bank account. You can see how conversion works on our convert crypto page.
  • Cross-border payments: stablecoins can move between countries in minutes, at any time of day.
  • Business settlement: merchants and platforms use them to settle payments and manage treasury balances. Read more about stablecoin settlement.

What are the risks?

"Stable" does not mean "risk-free". Before using any stablecoin, consider:

  • Issuer and reserve risk: the value depends on the issuer holding enough good-quality reserves and honouring redemptions.
  • De-pegging: in stressed markets a stablecoin can trade below its intended value, sometimes for a long period.
  • Regulatory risk: rules differ by country and are changing. In the European Union, the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) sets requirements for stablecoin issuers, which affects which stablecoins platforms can offer to EU users.
  • Technical and custody risk: sending to the wrong address or network, or losing access to a wallet, can mean losing funds.

How to choose a stablecoin

Look at who issues it, how its reserves are held and reported, whether it is available and permitted where you live, and which blockchain networks it runs on. Fees and transfer times also differ by network, so check the network before you send.

faq.q: Is a stablecoin the same as money in a bank?
faq.a: No. A stablecoin is a crypto-asset issued by a company. Its value depends on the issuer's reserves and redemption policy, and it is not covered by bank deposit protection schemes.

faq.q: Can a stablecoin lose its value?
faq.a: Yes. Stablecoins are designed to stay at their peg, but they can trade below it during market stress or if confidence in the issuer or its reserves falls.
They can move value across borders quickly and at any time, which helps with payments, settlement and treasury management between crypto and fiat.
